poster.title: Mexico 1968 Olympic Games
poster.creator: Lance Wyman and Eduardo Terrazas
poster.edition: Official Mexico 1968 Olympic poster; part of the programme directed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez. V&A E.338-2006.
poster.alt: Dense black and white parallel lines radiate from the Mexico 68 wordmark, with coloured Olympic rings integrated into the numerals.
poster.blurb: A wordmark grows into an entire optical field, binding the event name, date and Olympic rings together.

notes.title: Letters become landscape
notes.body: Parallel lines expand the contours of “Mexico” and “68” across the square. The background is generated by the lettering itself.

notes.title: A small colour signal
notes.body: The Olympic rings introduce colour into the dense black-and-white system. Their familiar shapes remain a point of recognition inside a demanding optical pattern.

notes.title: Repetition changes scale
notes.body: Close up, the image is a maze of thin stripes. From farther away, the event identity reappears. The poster rewards moving between those two distances.

studyData.intro: Start at the name, then let its parallel lines carry you to the edges. This almost square Olympic poster turns words, numerals and an emblem into one continuous field; the apparent movement comes from a still image.

regions.label: Mexico 68
regions.summary: The event name belongs to the pattern.

sections.heading: Read through the outlines
sections.body: The central line of lettering reads Mexico 68. Each character has several parallel edges rather than one solid stroke. The name remains readable, but its outlines also join the surrounding pattern, so identifying the word and following a line become different ways of looking.

sections.heading: An Olympic identity
sections.body: The V&A identifies this as an official poster for the 1968 Mexico City Olympic Games. It credits Lance Wyman and Eduardo Terrazas, and describes an identity developed under the direction of organising-committee president Pedro Ramírez Vázquez. Those credits concern a collaborative design programme.

regions.question: Where does reading a letter turn into following a pattern?

regions.label: Five linked rings
regions.summary: A familiar emblem is fitted into the numerals.

sections.heading: An emblem within a word
sections.body: Five interlinked rings sit inside the right-hand portion of the identity. Their blue, yellow, black, green and red introduce small colour accents into the otherwise dark-and-cream field. Circular contours rhyme with the rounded numerals around them, fitting a recognisable emblem into the larger line system.

sections.heading: The starting relationship
sections.body: The V&A explains that the Olympic rings helped generate the forms of 68, which were then extended into the Mexico lettering. This is a documented design relationship, not simply a resemblance noticed afterwards; the finished image lets you trace that integration.

regions.question: Which rings can you follow without slipping onto the numeral outlines?

regions.label: Lines to the edge
regions.summary: The identity spreads beyond its central band.

sections.heading: One interval, many turns
sections.body: Closely spaced dark and pale stripes fill the upper-left area. Their curves remain roughly parallel even as they change direction. That regular spacing allows a single bend to be repeated many times, turning a modest shape into a broad field of activity.

sections.heading: Motion without animation
sections.body: As your attention shifts between dark strokes and pale gaps, the surface may seem restless. The page itself stays still. Try attending to just one stripe: the experience changes from a busy overall texture to a slower, traceable route across the sheet.

regions.question: Can you follow one pale channel from the centre towards an edge?

regions.label: The numerals 68
regions.summary: A date also behaves like a set of loops.

sections.heading: A compressed date
sections.body: The two numerals share the height and outlined construction of the word Mexico. Their rounded enclosures sit close to the rings, while the remaining lettering uses a mixture of straight and curved routes. The year is part of the central identity rather than a separate caption.

sections.heading: Naming efficiently
sections.body: A place, a year and a sporting emblem provide a compact event identifier. There is no need to read a long paragraph before recognising the occasion. This describes what the poster offers visually; it does not establish how every viewer understood the campaign.

regions.question: What information would disappear if you covered only the numerals?

regions.label: The crossing strokes
regions.summary: An X-like junction interrupts the curves.

sections.heading: A different kind of route
sections.body: Near the middle-left, sloping parallel lines meet around the X in Mexico. These diagonals interrupt the rounded paths that dominate the right side. Small triangular pale spaces appear between the bundles, producing a sharper, more angular centre of activity.

sections.heading: A useful interruption
sections.body: If every line curved in the same way, the field could become harder to navigate. The crossing strokes offer a distinct landmark. Compare this area with the rings: both use repetition, but one gathers attention through a junction and the other through loops.

regions.question: Which is easier to find again after looking away: the crossing or the rings?

regions.label: Long descending strokes
regions.summary: The lower field stretches the name vertically.

sections.heading: From letters to stripes
sections.body: Below the left of the identity, long parallel strokes descend towards the bottom border. Their length greatly exceeds the height of the central letters. The same narrow spacing survives, so the extension reads as part of the lettering system rather than an unrelated background.

sections.heading: Changing the scale of a letter
sections.body: A small readable character becomes a large part of the page when its strokes continue outward. Cover the lower extension and the name feels more self-contained. Reveal it again and the lettering becomes a structure that organises the whole sheet.

regions.question: How does covering the lower stripes change the weight of the name?

regions.label: Rounded corners
regions.summary: The pattern turns instead of stopping.

sections.heading: A family of bends
sections.body: The upper-right corner contains a stack of rounded turns. Each line follows a similar path at a slightly different distance, like nested tracks. The curves carry the eye from a horizontal direction into a vertical one without adding another illustration or symbol.

sections.heading: Containing the energy
sections.body: These repeated turns make the field feel expansive and enclosed at once. Lines seem to travel outward from the identity, yet the bends bring them back into the rectangular sheet. Compare this controlled turning with the sharper crossing nearer the centre.

regions.question: Do the corner curves make your eye continue around the sheet or return inward?

regions.label: Pale gaps and paper
regions.summary: The light areas do as much work as the dark ones.

sections.heading: Two readable surfaces
sections.body: The pale channels between black strokes are consistent enough to form their own pattern. A narrow pale margin also separates the printed field from the outer edge. At this scale, foreground and background can exchange roles depending on which colour you choose to follow.

sections.heading: A reproduction is an object too
sections.body: The cream tone and small surface irregularities belong to the image available here. They should not be treated as a precise specification for the original paper or inks. Reading the pattern carefully does not require pretending this reproduction preserves every material detail.

regions.question: Can you see the pale channels as the main lines for a moment?

regions.label: One field, several traditions
regions.summary: A visual identity can carry more than a place name.

sections.heading: A museum account of its references
sections.body: The V&A relates the identity to contemporary Op Art and to pre-Hispanic and Huichol patterns. These are the museum’s documented connections. They do not make every curve a specific cultural symbol, or justify assigning a single meaning to all Mexican visual traditions.

sections.heading: A coordinated public face
sections.body: Because the word and pattern share a construction, parts of the image could remain recognisable at different scales. On this sheet, that unity gives the event a coherent visual presence. It is a reading of the design, not a claim about its measurable advertising success.

regions.question: Which part could you isolate while still recognising this particular identity?

sources.title: V&A: Official poster for the Mexico 1968 Olympic Games
sources.summary: Documents the official identity, credited collaborators, ring-to-numeral development and the museum’s account of design references.

studyData.transcriptNote: The central identity is transcribed. No tiny edge marks are expanded. This edition combines a dark-and-cream line field with coloured Olympic rings.

connections.label: Words become a field
connections.title: The lettering continues into its surroundings
connections.text: The central MEXICO68 reading and the surrounding parallel contours are visually continuous. Their separation is an analytical choice: bringing them together reveals how the wordmark shapes the whole field.

connections.label: Find the colour
connections.title: Five rings interrupt the optical rhythm
connections.text: The ring strokes cross the numerals within a mostly black-and-cream field. Their compact colour accents create a different point of attention inside the much larger pattern.
